<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2025-12" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2025-12 Assis and Brown v. South Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2025-12: Assis and Brown v. South Florida, M52GA" data-search-text="2025-12 Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. South Florida Presbytery Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s divestiture of their offices after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC reversed because their calls had never been formally dissolved, so they were not automatically without call, and BCO 34-10 did not apply while they remained actively engaged and accepted in ministry. The SJC could not judge their fairness and pretext claims from the record. It restored them to good standing and required Presbytery to dissolve the existing calls before pursuing lawful alternatives. appeal Sustained; Reversed Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment); Independent review (constitutional interpretation) — BCO 8-7, BCO 13-2, BCO 20-8, BCO 21-1, BCO 23-1, BCO 34-10, BCO 38-3.a, BCO 46-7 divestiture without censure ministerial status dissolution of pastoral call church withdrawal transfer of credentials presbytery jurisdiction">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2025-12</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga52_2025__2025-12_2025-13.html">Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. South Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained; Reversed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2025-12">Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s divestiture of their offices after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC reversed because their calls had never been formally dissolved, so they were not automatically without call, and BCO 34-10 did not apply while they remained actively engaged and accepted in ministry. The SJC could not judge their fairness and pretext claims from the record. It restored them to good standing and required Presbytery to dissolve the existing calls before pursuing lawful alternatives.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2025-12" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2025-13" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2025-13 Assis and Brown v. South Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2025-13: Assis and Brown v. South Florida, M52GA" data-search-text="2025-13 Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. South Florida Presbytery Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s decision to divest them of office without censure after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC sustained the BCO-violation specification and reversed the divestitures: their calls had never been formally dissolved, and BCO 34-10 did not apply because they continued performing ministerial functions and remained accepted by their churches. It declined as unable to judge claims that Presbytery disregarded their emails or used the procedure as discriminatory pretext. The ministers returned to good standing; Presbytery must dissolve their existing PCA calls and then pursue a BCO-consistent option. appeal Sustained; Reversed Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment); Independent review (constitutional interpretation) — BCO 8-7, BCO 13-2, BCO 20-8, BCO 21-1, BCO 23-1, BCO 34-10, BCO 38-3.a, BCO 46-7 divestiture without censure ministerial status dissolution of pastoral call church withdrawal transfer of credentials presbytery jurisdiction">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2025-13</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga52_2025__2025-12_2025-13.html">Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. South Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained; Reversed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2025-13">Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s decision to divest them of office without censure after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC sustained the BCO-violation specification and reversed the divestitures: their calls had never been formally dissolved, and BCO 34-10 did not apply because they continued performing ministerial functions and remained accepted by their churches. It declined as unable to judge claims that Presbytery disregarded their emails or used the procedure as discriminatory pretext. The ministers returned to good standing; Presbytery must dissolve their existing PCA calls and then pursue a BCO-consistent option.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2025-13" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-01" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-01 Hann v. Pee Dee" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-01: Hann v. Pee Dee, M51GA, p. 766" data-search-text="2023-01 Hann v. Pee Dee Presbytery Kristin Hann&#x27;s complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery was dismissed because the SJC held she lacked standing: she was not subject to Pee Dee Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction, so the complaint was judicially out of order and could not be put in order. The SJC made no merits ruling and stated that the ruling did not stay Presbytery&#x27;s continuing investigation or review of resulting actions. The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused. complaint Dismissed Not reached legacy 2023-1 BCO 46-8, BCO 43-1 standing to complain jurisdiction of presbytery complainant not subject to presbytery jurisdiction judicially out of order">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-01.html">Hann v. Pee Dee Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-01">Kristin Hann&#x27;s complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery was dismissed because the SJC held she lacked standing: she was not subject to Pee Dee Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction, so the complaint was judicially out of order and could not be put in order. The SJC made no merits ruling and stated that the ruling did not stay Presbytery&#x27;s continuing investigation or review of resulting actions. The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-02 Reynolds v. Pee Dee" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-02: Reynolds v. Pee Dee, M51GA, pp. 767–768" data-search-text="2023-02 Reynolds v. Pee Dee Presbytery The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds&#x27;s complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session&#x27;s reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2&#x27;s sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession. complaint Dismissed Not reached legacy 2023-2 BCO 43-2, BCO 31-5, BCO 39-3 timeliness of complaint sixty-day filing period judicially out of order standing personal offense injured party">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-02</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-02.html">Reynolds v. Pee Dee Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-02">The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds&#x27;s complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session&#x27;s reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2&#x27;s sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. The ruling expressly reserved whether Reynolds could proceed as an injured party under BCO 31-5 and whether the Session had jurisdiction over claims outside the received confession.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-04" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-04 Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-04: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley, M51GA, pp. 769–807" data-search-text="2023-04 Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 2023-4 BCO 40-1, BCO 40-2, BCO 40-2.2, BCO 40-2.3, BCO 40-3, BCO 40-4, BCO 40-5, BCO 40-6, BCO 15-4, BCO 14-6, BCO 33-1, BCO 39-1, BCO 39-3, BCO 43-1, BCO 34-1, BCO 43-8, BCO 43-3, BCO 11-4, BCO 32-18, BCO 31-2, BCO 3-2, BCO 3-4, BCO 35-14, BCO 13-1 Sabbath observance Super Bowl party review and control session records review SJC jurisdiction exception of substance Westminster Confession 21:8 WLC 117 WLC 118 BCO 40-2 BCO 40-3 non-justiciability adjacent courts RAO Chapter 16">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-04</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-04.html">Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-04">Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-04" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-05 Hyland v. Chicago Metro" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-05: Hyland v. Chicago Metro, M52GA, pp. 810–817" data-search-text="2023-05 Hyland v. Chicago Metro Presbytery Former church employee Emily Hyland complained to the SJC after Chicago Metro Presbytery ruled her BCO 43 complaint out of order because, as a local-church member, she was not subject to Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction. The SJC was equally divided 12–12–0 on the proposed panel decision, so CMP&#x27;s ruling stands. That proposed decision would have answered that CMP did not err: Hyland lacked standing to file a BCO 43-1 complaint with Presbytery. No amendments were made. An evenly divided SJC thus leaves the lower ruling in place without a majority rationale. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 2023-5 BCO 43-1, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-2 standing to complain employment termination BCO 43-1 standing church employee accusations against teaching elders judicially out of order civil authorities">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga52_2025__2023-05.html">Hyland v. Chicago Metro Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-05">Former church employee Emily Hyland complained to the SJC after Chicago Metro Presbytery ruled her BCO 43 complaint out of order because, as a local-church member, she was not subject to Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction. The SJC was equally divided 12–12–0 on the proposed panel decision, so CMP&#x27;s ruling stands. That proposed decision would have answered that CMP did not err: Hyland lacked standing to file a BCO 43-1 complaint with Presbytery. No amendments were made. An evenly divided SJC thus leaves the lower ruling in place without a majority rationale.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-05" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-06" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-06 Baird et al. v. Grace" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-06: Baird et al. v. Grace, M51GA, pp. 789–807" data-search-text="2023-06 Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a mediation complaint, investigative directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a trial stay. The SJC held that the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; official-record requests were proper, but compelling nonrecord personal communications and requiring the Session to address its congregation exceeded Presbytery’s authority. It vacated the communications directive and annulled the stay for lack of the required prior citation. It upheld committee examination of the BCO 40-5 reports and did not reach alleged partiality; the Session trials were to proceed. complaint Partially sustained; Denied; Moot Not stated legacy 2023-6 BCO 40-5 complaint procedure BCO 40-5 review document production stay of judicial proceedings mootness">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-06</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-06_2023-08.html">Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained; Denied; Moot</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-06">Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a mediation complaint, investigative directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a trial stay. The SJC held that the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; official-record requests were proper, but compelling nonrecord personal communications and requiring the Session to address its congregation exceeded Presbytery’s authority. It vacated the communications directive and annulled the stay for lack of the required prior citation. It upheld committee examination of the BCO 40-5 reports and did not reach alleged partiality; the Session trials were to proceed.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-06" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-07" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-07 Evans v. Arizona" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-07: Evans v. Arizona, M51GA, pp. 808–823" data-search-text="2023-07 Evans v. Arizona Presbytery Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. It directed Presbytery to record the irregular withdrawal, acknowledge his new membership, and remove him from its roll. appeal Sustained; Reversed Not stated legacy 2023-7 BCO 23-1, BCO 13-2, BCO 13-6, BCO 34-10, BCO 38-3.a, BCO 38-3.b, BCO 2-2, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-3, BCO 42-9, BCO 38-3, BCO 40-5, BCO 43-1, BCO 38-3.2 withdrawal from denomination BCO 38-3a divestiture without censure jurisdiction over withdrawing minister teaching elder without call transfer to another denomination standing to appeal removal from presbytery roll">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-07</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-07.html">Evans v. Arizona Presbytery</a></h3></header>

<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-07">Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-08" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-08 Baird et al. v. Grace" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-08: Baird et al. v. Grace, M51GA, pp. 789–807" data-search-text="2023-08 Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a withdrawn mediation complaint, document and congregational-notice directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a stay of Session trials. The SJC sustained the complaints in the main: the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; Presbytery could require official record materials but not compel personal communications or force the Session to address its congregation; and the stay lacked a prior BCO 40-5 citation. It upheld appointing a committee to examine the reports, did not reach alleged partiality, vacated the overbroad directive, annulled the stay, and returned the trials to Session. complaint Partially sustained; Denied Not stated legacy 2023-8 BCO 40-5 complaint procedure BCO 40-5 review document production stay of judicial proceedings mootness">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-08</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-06_2023-08.html">Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained; Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-08">Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a withdrawn mediation complaint, document and congregational-notice directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a stay of Session trials. The SJC sustained the complaints in the main: the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; Presbytery could require official record materials but not compel personal communications or force the Session to address its congregation; and the stay lacked a prior BCO 40-5 citation. It upheld appointing a committee to examine the reports, did not reach alleged partiality, vacated the overbroad directive, annulled the stay, and returned the trials to Session.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-08" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-09" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-09 Myers v. Illiana" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-09: Myers v. Illiana, M51GA, pp. 824–855" data-search-text="2023-09 Myers v. Illiana Presbytery An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. The SJC granted the appeal, reversed in whole, and remanded, restoring the prior suspensions. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-10" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-10 Martinez and Cook v. Pacific" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-10: Martinez and Cook v. Pacific, M51GA, pp. 856–866" data-search-text="2023-10 Martinez &amp; Cook v. Pacific Presbytery Elders challenged Presbytery’s authority and vague instruction for its Shepherding Committee to “follow up” with their Session. The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. It did not decide the underlying doxology dispute or order further relief. complaint Partially sustained Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment) — BCO 11-4, BCO 13-9, BCO 13-9.f, BCO 13-9.g, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.1, BCO 39-3.3, BCO 39-3.4, BCO 13-1, BCO 43-1, BCO 52-2 presbytery visitation shepherding committee session oversight presbytery jurisdiction BCO 13-9 BCO 11-4 doxology worship service elements complaint procedure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-10</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-10.html">Martinez &amp; Cook v. Pacific Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-10">Elders challenged Presbytery’s authority and vague instruction for its Shepherding Committee to “follow up” with their Session. The SJC denied the constitutional challenge because the record reasonably supported concern for the church’s peace and spiritual welfare, but sustained the challenge to Presbytery’s lack of specific direction and poor communication. The decision distinguishes prohibited mandatory visitation without cause from a reasonably justified visit, while requiring clarity about its objectives. It did not decide the underlying doxology dispute or order further relief.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-10" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-11" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-11 Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-11: Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest, M51GA, pp. 867–908" data-search-text="2023-11 Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution. complaint Sustained Not stated — BCO 3-1, BCO 4-1, BCO 5-9, BCO 5-10, BCO 6-2, BCO 6-4, BCO 11-3, BCO 16-1, BCO 16-2, BCO 20-2, BCO 20-3, BCO 20-4, BCO 20-5, BCO 24-1, BCO 24-3, BCO 24-7, BCO 25-1, BCO 25-2, BCO 25-3, BCO 25-7, BCO 25-11, BCO 25-12, BCO 27-3, BCO 28-1, BCO 28-3, BCO 43-1, BCO 46-3, BCO 46-4, BCO 57-2, BCO 57-5, BCO 58-4, BCO 14-2, BCO 10-1, BCO 13-10, BCO 19-16, BCO 21-5, BCO 23-1, BCO 21-4.a, BCO 13-3, BCO 25-4, BCO 34-10, BCO 24-10 minor communicant voting congregational meeting voting rights good and regular standing church bylaws officer election communicant membership BCO 6-4 BCO 20-3 BCO 24-3 BCO 25-1 age restrictions session authority">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-11</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-11.html">Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-11">The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-11" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-13" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-13 BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-13: BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY, M51GA, pp. 909–941" data-search-text="2023-13 BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery&#x27;s failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord&#x27;s Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session&#x27;s later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church&#x27;s session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly&#x27;s direct referral but did not void it. bco_40_5_matter Remanded Not reached — BCO 40-5 women preaching public worship sermon requirements presbytery discipline review of presbytery records institutional procedure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-13</code> <span>· BCO 40-5 matter</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-13.html">BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-13">A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery&#x27;s failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord&#x27;s Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session&#x27;s later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church&#x27;s session and report to the 51st General Assembly. A separate procedural note questioned the Assembly&#x27;s direct referral but did not void it.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-13" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-14" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-14 BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-14: BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia, M51GA, pp. 941–952" data-search-text="2023-14 BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy&#x27;s legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded. bco_40_5_matter Other; Denied BCO 40-5 — important delinquency or grossly unconstitutional proceeding — BCO 40-5, BCO 20-4, BCO 20-5, BCO 24-7, BCO 15-4, BCO 15-1, BCO 14-6, BCO 40-1, BCO 11-3, BCO 25-11, BCO 34-4, BCO 43-1 BCO 40-5 delinquency congregational election procedure slate voting ballot vs. standing vote associate pastor installation unauthorized commission call to ministry presbytery oversight">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-14</code> <span>· BCO 40-5 matter</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-14.html">BCO 40-5 Matter re NW Georgia</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Other; Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-14">Presbytery approved calls and installed three associate pastors after a constitutionally deficient election. The SJC found egregious error, including slate voting, a standing rather than ballot vote, and failure to determine and record the number of voters present under the then-current rule. It nevertheless denied the requested annulment of the installations because PCA judicial proceedings supplied no precedent and the remedy&#x27;s legitimacy was doubtful. The SJC stayed further proceedings and declared the report concluded.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-14" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

South Florida, M51GA, pp. 946–951" data-search-text="2023-15 Tom Turner v. South Florida Presbytery Turner complained against Presbytery Judicial Commission actions deposing TE Tommy Boland and dissolving Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery. The SJC ruled both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing and incapable of being put in order. Cross Community had already disaffiliated through its first congregational motion; the second motion, which contemplated later implementation, was out of order as contingent. Because no Presbytery action was required to effect disaffiliation, Turner was no longer a PCA member. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-15</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-15_2023-17.html">Tom Turner v. South Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Administratively out of order</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-15">Turner complained against Presbytery Judicial Commission actions deposing TE Tommy Boland and dissolving Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery. The SJC ruled both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing and incapable of being put in order. Cross Community had already disaffiliated through its first congregational motion; the second motion, which contemplated later implementation, was out of order as contingent. Because no Presbytery action was required to effect disaffiliation, Turner was no longer a PCA member. The underlying challenges were not decided.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-15" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-17" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-17 Turner v. South Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-17: Turner v. South Florida, M51GA, pp. 946–951" data-search-text="2023-17 Tom Turner v. South Florida Presbytery Turner’s two complaints challenged the deposition of TE Tommy Boland and the dissolution of Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery, although the record does not identify which challenge was Case 2023-17. In a combined ruling, the SJC held both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing. The congregation’s first withdrawal vote immediately satisfied BCO 25-11; its second, contingent timing motion was out of order. Because the church had already left the PCA, Turner was no longer a member, and no merits relief was available. complaint Administratively out of order Not reached — BCO 25-11 standing church disaffiliation administratively out of order complaint procedure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-17</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-15_2023-17.html">Tom Turner v. South Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Administratively out of order</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-17">Turner’s two complaints challenged the deposition of TE Tommy Boland and the dissolution of Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery, although the record does not identify which challenge was Case 2023-17. In a combined ruling, the SJC held both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing. The congregation’s first withdrawal vote immediately satisfied BCO 25-11; its second, contingent timing motion was out of order. Because the church had already left the PCA, Turner was no longer a member, and no merits relief was available.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-17" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-19" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2023-19 Huffman v. Tennessee Valley" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2023-19: Huffman v. Tennessee Valley, M51GA, pp. 952–968" data-search-text="2023-19 Huffman v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery A filing challenging Presbytery’s handling of Huffman’s BCO 38-1 confession was styled as an appeal under a newly amended rule. The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided. appeal Judicially out of order; Remanded Not reached — BCO 31-2, BCO 38-1, BCO 43-2, BCO 42-5, BCO 42-7, BCO 43-6, BCO 32-18, BCO 42-9, BCO 42-3, BCO 35-7, BCO 35-8.35, BCO 35-14 BCO 38-1 case without process retroactive application of amended BCO complaint vs. appeal confession of sin judicially out of order remand 50th General Assembly BCO amendment">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-19</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2023-19.html">Huffman v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Judicially out of order; Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2023-19">A filing challenging Presbytery’s handling of Huffman’s BCO 38-1 confession was styled as an appeal under a newly amended rule. The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2023-19" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-01" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-01 Eagle v. Savannah River" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-01: Eagle v. Savannah River, M49GA, pp. 948–949" data-search-text="2022-01 Eagle v. Savannah River Presbytery The SJC dismissed Eric Eagle and others&#x27; complaint against Savannah River Presbytery as administratively out of order and untimely under BCO 43-3. The complaint was first filed prematurely in December 2020; after the SJC reset the filing clock to the later of its October 21, 2021 action or Presbytery&#x27;s October 20, 2020 ruling, it was filed more than 30 days later. The merits were not reached. An attached SJC response to CCB separately defended its record-reopening in Case 2020-12 and asked CCB to deny an exception request as untimely, waived, and procedural. complaint Administratively out of order; Dismissed Not reached legacy 2022-1 BCO 43-3 administratively out of order untimely complaint BCO 43-3 thirty-day filing deadline complaint timing untimely filing BCO 43-3 timeliness complaint procedure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga49_2022__2022-01.html">Eagle v. Savannah River Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Administratively out of order; Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-01">The SJC dismissed Eric Eagle and others&#x27; complaint against Savannah River Presbytery as administratively out of order and untimely under BCO 43-3. The complaint was first filed prematurely in December 2020; after the SJC reset the filing clock to the later of its October 21, 2021 action or Presbytery&#x27;s October 20, 2020 ruling, it was filed more than 30 days later. The merits were not reached. An attached SJC response to CCB separately defended its record-reopening in Case 2020-12 and asked CCB to deny an exception request as untimely, waived, and procedural.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-03" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-03 Klett et al. v. Philadelphia" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-03: Klett et al. v. Philadelphia, M50GA, pp. 812–824" data-search-text="2022-03 Klett et al. v. Philadelphia Presbytery Philadelphia Presbytery declared that TE Larry Smith&#x27;s views on continuing prophecy and tongues were not out of accord or hostile to the system of doctrine. Klett et al. complained. The SJC sustained the complaint: Smith&#x27;s written views affirmed continuing non-general revelation and treated prophecy and tongues as public-worship elements, contrary to WCF 1 and 21, so Presbytery erred under BCO 21-4.f. The SJC annulled Presbytery&#x27;s May 15, 2021 action. No further action was possible because Smith and his congregation had left the PCA; the matter was concluded, with precedent limited to the written views reviewed. complaint Sustained Not stated legacy 2022-3 BCO 13-6, BCO 21-4.e, BCO 21-4.f, BCO 21-4, BCO 7-1 continuing gifts of prophecy and tongues cessationism continuationism fundamentals of the system of doctrine hostile to the system Westminster Confession of Faith 1.1 Westminster Confession of Faith 1.6 BCO 21-4.f new revelation teaching elder examination exception to standards transfer of minister spiritual gifts">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-03</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-03.html">Klett et al. v. Philadelphia Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-03">Philadelphia Presbytery declared that TE Larry Smith&#x27;s views on continuing prophecy and tongues were not out of accord or hostile to the system of doctrine. Klett et al. complained. The SJC sustained the complaint: Smith&#x27;s written views affirmed continuing non-general revelation and treated prophecy and tongues as public-worship elements, contrary to WCF 1 and 21, so Presbytery erred under BCO 21-4.f. The SJC annulled Presbytery&#x27;s May 15, 2021 action. No further action was possible because Smith and his congregation had left the PCA; the matter was concluded, with precedent limited to the written views reviewed.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-03" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-04" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-04 Sheppard v. Highlands" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-04: Sheppard v. Highlands, M50GA, pp. 825–850" data-search-text="2022-04 Sheppard v. Highlands Presbytery The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard&#x27;s complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused&#x27;s right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20&#x27;s one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling. complaint Sustained Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment) legacy 2022-4 BCO 31-2, BCO 32-20, BCO 11-3, BCO 11-4, BCO 14-3, BCO 14-7, BCO 27-1, BCO 27-2, BCO 27-3, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.2, BCO 39-3.3, BCO 31-3, BCO 13-2, BCO 34-10, BCO 40-5, BCO 32-20.18 timeliness of process BCO 32-20 statute of limitations strong presumption of guilt BCO 31-2 mandatory process judicial and pastoral procedures case of scandal retroactive application of BCO amendments debarment from prosecution stare decisis in ecclesiastical courts">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-04</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-04.html">Sheppard v. Highlands Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-04">The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard&#x27;s complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused&#x27;s right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20&#x27;s one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-04" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-05 Crouse et al. v. Northwest Georgia" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-05: Crouse et al. v. Northwest Georgia, M50GA, pp. 851–852" data-search-text="2022-05 Crouse et al. v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery Three Ruling Elders complained of errors in judicial process against them. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot because the Session had dismissed every charge and ended the process, while the elders had voluntarily resigned and requested dissolution of their calls. Because these events removed the challenged action and settled the underlying dispute, the SJC did not reach the alleged procedural errors. complaint Out of order (type not stated); Moot Not reached legacy 2022-5 BCO 32-20 mootness out of order judicial process dismissed ruling elder discipline complaint moot charges dismissed standing ruling elders">

<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Out of order (type not stated); Moot</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">

<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-05">Three Ruling Elders complained of errors in judicial process against them. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-07" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-07 Harrell et al. v. Covenant" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-07: Harrell et al. v. Covenant, M50GA, pp. 852–882" data-search-text="2022-07 Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister&#x27;s expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery&#x27;s affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected. appeal Sustained; Reversed Great deference unless clear error (factual findings) legacy 2022-7 BCO 5-1, BCO 5-5.a, BCO 5-9.f, BCO 5-9.f.1, BCO 5-10, BCO 16-1, BCO 16-2, BCO 20-2, BCO 27-3, BCO 29-1, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-5, BCO 35-11, BCO 36-5, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.2, BCO 39-3.4, BCO 39-1.3, BCO 40-5, BCO 41-5, BCO 42-5, BCO 57-5, BCO 39-3.3, BCO 32-3 indictment specificity sufficiency of indictment BCO 32-5 times places circumstances mission church polity congregational right to select minister organizing pastor election fifth commandment ninth commandment disqualification of judges standard of review in appeals provisional Session authority particularization of mission church BCO 31-2 investigation due process mission church particularization congregational rights minister selection witnesses as judges contumacy location of trial reference to presbytery membership vows slander organizing pastor">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-07</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-07.html">Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained; Reversed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-07">The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister&#x27;s expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery&#x27;s affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-07" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Pittsburgh Presbytery The SJC held that RE David Snoke&#x27;s complaint against Pittsburgh Presbytery&#x27;s January 29, 2022 action was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because Snoke, not a commissioner from his church to that meeting, lacked standing to complain. Although Presbytery later voted 20-16-3 to find the complaint in order, the SJC said it should have been ruled out of order. The SJC did not reach the merits. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-08</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-08.html">David Snoke v. Pittsburgh Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> No final disposition in available record</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-08">The SJC held that RE David Snoke&#x27;s complaint against Pittsburgh Presbytery&#x27;s January 29, 2022 action was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because Snoke, not a commissioner from his church to that meeting, lacked standing to complain. Although Presbytery later voted 20-16-3 to find the complaint in order, the SJC said it should have been ruled out of order. The SJC did not reach the merits. Its vote was 20-1, with three absent.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-08" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-09" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-09 Benyola v. Central Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-09: Benyola v. Central Florida, M50GA, pp. 883–910" data-search-text="2022-09 Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery The SJC declared Benyola&#x27;s complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers&#x27; recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint&#x27;s merits, so the case&#x27;s value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination. complaint No final disposition in available record Not reached legacy 2022-9 BCO 31-2, BCO 41-2, BCO 43-9, BCO 43-10, BCO 21-4.1a, BCO 31-10, BCO 32-3, BCO 41-3, BCO 31-7, BCO 35-1, BCO 21-5 standing church membership complaint out of order administrative dismissal">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-09</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-09.html">Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> No final disposition in available record</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-09">The SJC declared Benyola&#x27;s complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. The decision was adopted 23-0 on a roll call, one absent, on the officers&#x27; recommendation. The record does not identify the underlying presbytery action or reach the complaint&#x27;s merits, so the case&#x27;s value is its threshold standing ruling, not any complaint determination.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-09" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-10" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-10 Presbyterian Church in America v. TE Daniel Herron" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-10: Presbyterian Church in America v. TE Daniel Herron, M50GA, pp. 884–917" data-search-text="2022-10 Presbyterian Church in America v. TE Daniel Herron On a BCO 41 reference, the SJC tried a minister on seven charges arising from allegations of sexual misconduct, bullying, dishonesty, a civil defamation suit, contumacy, doctrinal error, and lack of fitness. It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful. judicial_reference Not guilty Not stated — BCO 31-2, BCO 31-7, BCO 31-10, BCO 32-3, BCO 34-1, BCO 35-1, BCO 41-2, BCO 41-3, BCO 43-9, BCO 43-10 trial by SJC reference sexual harassment civil lawsuit by minister 1 Corinthians 6 defamation lawsuit contumacy investigating committee BCO 31-2 investigation suspension from office church planting acquittal restoration to standing witness testimony">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-10</code> <span>· Judicial reference</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-10.html">Presbyterian Church in America v. TE Daniel Herron</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not guilty</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-10">On a BCO 41 reference, the SJC tried a minister on seven charges arising from allegations of sexual misconduct, bullying, dishonesty, a civil defamation suit, contumacy, doctrinal error, and lack of fitness. It found him not guilty on every charge because the prosecution failed to meet its burden, removed all censures and administrative suspensions, and restored him to good standing. For the lawsuit charge, it rejected a categorical ban on civil suits between Christians and required proof that this suit was sinful.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-10" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-11" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-11 BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Central Indiana" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-11: BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Central Indiana, M50GA, p. 918" data-search-text="2022-11 BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Central Indiana Presbytery The SJC had postponed BCO 34-1 petitions concerning Central Indiana Presbytery until the Herron trial concluded. After acquitting Herron on all charges and restoring him to good standing, the SJC answered and decided the petitions by reference to that final trial decision. The petitions were thus resolved through incorporation of the trial result, not transferred to another court; the trial itself arose from a distinct BCO 41 reference. original_jurisdiction_request Other Not reached — BCO 34-1 original jurisdiction BCO 34-1 petitions postponement pending trial Central Indiana Presbytery Herron related matters">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-11</code> <span>· Original-jurisdiction request</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-11.html">BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Central Indiana Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Other</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-11">The SJC had postponed BCO 34-1 petitions concerning Central Indiana Presbytery until the Herron trial concluded. After acquitting Herron on all charges and restoring him to good standing, the SJC answered and decided the petitions by reference to that final trial decision. The petitions were thus resolved through incorporation of the trial result, not transferred to another court; the trial itself arose from a distinct BCO 41 reference.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-11" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-12" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-12 BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Missouri" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-12: BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Missouri, M50GA, pp. 919–922" data-search-text="2022-12 BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Missouri Presbytery The SJC dismissed two BCO 34-1 overtures asking the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction over alleged doctrinal errors by TE Greg Johnson. After Memorial Presbyterian Church withdrew from the PCA and Missouri Presbytery removed Johnson&#x27;s name from its rolls under BCO 38-3a, the SJC held it lacked authority to assume original jurisdiction because the PCA no longer had jurisdiction over him. The dismissal did not resolve the doctrinal allegations; one commissioner dissented. original_jurisdiction_request Dismissed Not reached — BCO 34-1, BCO 38-3.a, BCO 31-2, BCO 38-3 original jurisdiction BCO 34-1 petitions loss of jurisdiction withdrawal from PCA doctrinal error same-sex attraction Revoice Missouri Presbytery Greg Johnson Memorial Presbyterian Church">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-12</code> <span>· Original-jurisdiction request</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-12.html">BCO 34-1 Petitions re: Missouri Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-12">The SJC dismissed two BCO 34-1 overtures asking the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction over alleged doctrinal errors by TE Greg Johnson. After Memorial Presbyterian Church withdrew from the PCA and Missouri Presbytery removed Johnson&#x27;s name from its rolls under BCO 38-3a, the SJC held it lacked authority to assume original jurisdiction because the PCA no longer had jurisdiction over him. The dismissal did not resolve the doctrinal allegations; one commissioner dissented.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-12" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order: that letter triggered BCO 43-1’s 60-day deadline, but Miller filed with the Session on November 20, 2021, and no new Session action occurred within the preceding 60 days. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-13</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-13.html">Miller v. Hills &amp; Plains Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-13">Wade Miller challenged his Session’s May 19, 2021 letter standing by its decision to permit a non-church yoga class to meet on church property. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order: that letter triggered BCO 43-1’s 60-day deadline, but Miller filed with the Session on November 20, 2021, and no new Session action occurred within the preceding 60 days. Citing a one-day-late precedent, the SJC reached no merits.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-13" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-16" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-16 Michelson et al. v. Northwest Georgia" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-16: Michelson et al. v. Northwest Georgia, M50GA, pp. 924–925" data-search-text="2022-16 Michelson et al. v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery The SJC declined to reach a complaint arising from judicial process against three ruling elders (not the complainants), because the Session dismissed all charges and ended that process on July 23, 2022, and the elders resigned and their calls were dissolved. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot, with no merits ruling, and approved the decision 23-0. The case illustrates that termination of the underlying judicial process and voluntary resignations can moot a complaint about that process. complaint Out of order (type not stated); Dismissed; Moot Not reached — None listed complaint out of order moot charges dismissed judicial process ruling elders">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-16</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga50_2023__2022-16.html">Michelson et al. v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Out of order (type not stated); Dismissed; Moot</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-16">The SJC declined to reach a complaint arising from judicial process against three ruling elders (not the complainants), because the Session dismissed all charges and ended that process on July 23, 2022, and the elders resigned and their calls were dissolved. The SJC found the complaint out of order and moot, with no merits ruling, and approved the decision 23-0. The case illustrates that termination of the underlying judicial process and voluntary resignations can moot a complaint about that process.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-16" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-21" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-21 Senters v. Savannah River" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-21: Senters v. Savannah River, M51GA, pp. 714–725" data-search-text="2022-21 Senters v. Savannah River Presbytery A minister challenged Presbytery’s procedures and its classification of a transfer candidate’s views on continuing tongues as “not a difference.” The SJC rejected the procedural objections because Presbytery could disregard its committee’s recommendation and had breached no required procedure. It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable. complaint Partially sustained; Remanded Not stated — BCO 13-6, BCO 19-2, BCO 21-4, BCO 21-4.e, BCO 21-4.f, BCO 15-1, BCO 7-1 transfer examination stated differences Westminster Confession of Faith gift of tongues continuationism cessationism WCF 1.1 WCF 1.6 WCF 21.3 presbytery examination procedures">

Savannah River Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained; Remanded</p>

It nevertheless held that a difference need not overtly contradict the Standards and that the candidate’s statements implicated WCF 1.1 and 1.6. It annulled the classification and remanded for clarification and a new judgment, without deciding whether the clarified view would be acceptable.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-21" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-22" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-22 Turner v. South Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-22: Turner v. South Florida, M51GA, pp. 726–741" data-search-text="2022-22 Turner v. South Florida Presbytery Presbytery investigated a Session&#x27;s handling of sexual-misconduct allegations and found it guilty of delinquencies without a trial. The SJC upheld Presbytery&#x27;s authority to receive credible reports and investigate, but annulled the findings of guilt, censures, and corrective mandates because BCO 40-6 required formal process or an admission before censure. It returned the matter for records review, informal resolution, or formal process and declined interim mandates that would assume the disputed allegations were true. complaint Partially sustained; Annulled; Remanded Not stated — BCO 12-7, BCO 13-9.f, BCO 13-9.e, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-6, BCO 40-4, BCO 40-5, BCO 40-6, BCO 43-10, BCO 13-9 sexual abuse session delinquency judicial commission authority BCO 40-5 BCO 40-4 due process indictment trial presbytery oversight of sessions important delinquency credible reports insubordination">

<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-22">Presbytery investigated a Session&#x27;s handling of sexual-misconduct allegations and found it guilty of delinquencies without a trial. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-23" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2022-23 Woodham v. South Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2022-23: Woodham v. South Florida, M51GA, pp. 742–767" data-search-text="2022-23 Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery&#x27;s efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority&#x27;s broad reasoning and deference. complaint Denied Great deference unless clear error (factual findings; discretion and judgment) — BCO 30-1, BCO 30-3, BCO 30-5, BCO 33-1, BCO 34-4, BCO 34-7, BCO 36-7, BCO 37-8, BCO 37-9, BCO 38-1, BCO 38-4, BCO 39-3, BCO 46-3, BCO 46-6, BCO 46-8, BCO 5-9, BCO 11-4, BCO 5-9.c, BCO 1-3, BCO 37-9.b, BCO 37-9.a, BCO 34-4.b, BCO 39-3.2, BCO 43-2, BCO 31-5 deposition excommunication BCO 46-8 presbytery jurisdiction over deposed minister assignment to particular church censure jurisdiction BCO 37-9 BCO 37-8 post-deposition discipline">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-23</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga51_2024__2022-23.html">Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2022-23">South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery&#x27;s jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery&#x27;s efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority&#x27;s broad reasoning and deference.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2022-23" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Northwest Georgia, M49GA, pp. 740–741" data-search-text="2021-01 Michelson v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery The SJC held that Stuart Michelson&#x27;s complaint against Northwest Georgia Presbytery was administratively out of order because he filed it with the SJC before Presbytery had completed its hearing on the complaint. The SJC did not reach the merits. It reset Michelson&#x27;s time to elevate the complaint to run from the later of notification of the SJC&#x27;s action or Presbytery&#x27;s ruling on the complaint. <p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> No final disposition in available record</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2021-01">The SJC held that Stuart Michelson&#x27;s complaint against Northwest Georgia Presbytery was administratively out of order because he filed it with the SJC before Presbytery had completed its hearing on the complaint. <p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> No final disposition in available record</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2021-02">In this BCO 40-5 request, the SJC advised the Stated Clerk that Tippins v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery should be referred to the General Assembly&#x27;s Review of Presbytery Records Committee. The SJC approved that action 19-3-0; three commissioners dissented. The sparse record supplies no underlying facts, merits analysis, or reason for the referral.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2021-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2021-03" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2021-03 DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2021-03: DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church, M49GA, pp. 878–883" data-search-text="2021-03 DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan. complaint Partially sustained Not stated legacy 2021-3 BCO 43-1, BCO 15-1, BCO 15-2, BCO 15-3, BCO 15-4, BCO 15-5, BCO 12-5 session governance commission judicial commission ecclesiastical commission BCO 15 commissions ruling elder term limits bylaw amendment congregational governance scope of commission authority standing commission ecclesiastical commissions governance commission session authority elder terms of office ruling elder governance">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2021-03</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga49_2022__2021-03.html">DeJong v. Session of Village Seven Presbyterian Church</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2021-03">A ruling elder challenged Session’s elder-term proposal and its creation of Judicial and Governance Commissions. The SJC denied the first two claims: the Constitution does not regulate elder terms, and the Judicial Commission’s assigned business was sufficiently defined. It sustained the Governance Commission claim because sweeping authority and reversed delegation allowed that body to function as Session itself, contrary to BCO 15-1. Session’s third motion was annulled, but Session remained free to adopt a narrower, constitutionally compliant plan.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2021-03" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2021-06" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="2021-06 Herron et al. v. Central Indiana" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 2021-06: Herron et al. v. Central Indiana, M49GA, pp. 916–934" data-search-text="2021-06 Herron et al. v. Central Indiana Presbytery Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. <div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2021-06">Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2021-08</code> <span>· Review and control</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga49_2022__2021-08.html">In re Korean Southwest Orange County Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> No final disposition in available record</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-2021-08">As of March 3, 2022, Presbytery had not supplied formally adopted responses to records-review exceptions, although its clerk had prepared drafts. The SJC allowed time for adoption and filing by April 1, after which it would forward the responses for records review; failure to file would prompt a called hearing. This was an unfinished compliance process, not approval of the draft responses or a final merits decision.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-2021-08" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>
