<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1998-02 St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1998-02: St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida, M27GA, pp. 79–90" data-search-text="1998-02 St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications. complaint Denied Great deference unless clear error (factual findings) legacy 1998-2 BCO 15-3, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-2, BCO 34-1, BCO 34-3, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.2, BCO 43-1 investigation disciplinary process commission procedure reasonable indulgence prejudice charges against teaching elder strong presumption of guilt judicial commission congregational complaint">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1998-02</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga27_1999__1998-02.html">St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1998-02">The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1998-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1998-05 Long, et al. v. James River" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1998-05: Long, et al. v. James River, M27GA, pp. 73–77" data-search-text="1998-05 Long, et al. v. James River Presbytery At issue was whether James River Presbytery erred by instructing TE Andrew Conrad not to teach or preach his views that the Genesis days were not necessarily six twenty-four-hour days, after JRP treated the views as an exception. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving JRP&#x27;s instruction in effect. It deferred under BCO 39-3, finding no significant procedural or constitutional error and no clear error of discretion; the parties had stipulated that instruction as the sole issue. The eight dissenters would have found JRP exceeded its discretion. complaint Denied Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment) legacy 1998-5 BCO 43-4, BCO 39-3, BCO 11-4, BCO 27-37, BCO 11-2 creation days anthropomorphic days ordination exception teaching and preaching restriction liberty of conscience presbytery authority exceptions to confessional standards Genesis 1">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1998-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga27_1999__1998-05.html">Long, et al. v. James River Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1998-05">At issue was whether James River Presbytery erred by instructing TE Andrew Conrad not to teach or preach his views that the Genesis days were not necessarily six twenty-four-hour days, after JRP treated the views as an exception. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving JRP&#x27;s instruction in effect. It deferred under BCO 39-3, finding no significant procedural or constitutional error and no clear error of discretion; the parties had stipulated that instruction as the sole issue. The eight dissenters would have found JRP exceeded its discretion.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1998-05" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-08" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1998-08 Smith v. Southwest" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1998-08: Smith v. Southwest, M28GA, pp. 218–229" data-search-text="1998-08 Smith v. Southwest Presbytery Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient. appeal Sustained; Reversed Not stated legacy 1998-8 BCO 33-4, BCO 34-3, BCO 35-3, BCO 31-2, BCO 31-3, BCO 31-9, BCO 32-6, BCO 33-2, BCO 34-4, BCO 39-3, BCO 40-5, BCO 42-6, BCO 43-7, BCO 43-8, BCO 43-9, BCO 31-10 appeal discipline evidence witnesses burden of proof presumption of guilt contumacy suspension from sacraments procedural errors factiousness slander divisiveness membership vows case in process panel">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1998-08</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga28_2000__1998-08.html">Smith v. Southwest Presbytery</a></h3></header>

<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1998-08">Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1998-08" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-09" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1998-09 Baer v. Illiana" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1998-09: Baer v. Illiana, M28GA, pp. 229–235" data-search-text="1998-09 Baer v. Illiana Presbytery An appeal from a Presbytery judgment and indefinite suspension of a pastor turned on whether he violated the Ninth Commandment and ordination/installation vows by telling the congregation the Session had &#x27;demanded&#x27; his resignation for six weeks. The SJC denied the appeal, holding the Session as a whole had not formally demanded resignation; individual elders&#x27; earlier opinions did not excuse the overstatement, which harmed the Session&#x27;s good name. It also found no due-process irregularity or prejudice warranting reversal, deferring to the lower court under BCO 39-3, leaving indefinite suspension in place. appeal Denied Great deference unless clear error (factual findings) legacy 1998-9 BCO 31-7, BCO 39-3 appeal pastoral discipline indefinite suspension 9th commandment ordination vows installation vows pastoral relationship false statements congregational meeting pastoral resignation case in process panel">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1998-09</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga28_2000__1998-09.html">Baer v. Illiana Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1998-09">An appeal from a Presbytery judgment and indefinite suspension of a pastor turned on whether he violated the Ninth Commandment and ordination/installation vows by telling the congregation the Session had &#x27;demanded&#x27; his resignation for six weeks. The SJC denied the appeal, holding the Session as a whole had not formally demanded resignation; individual elders&#x27; earlier opinions did not excuse the overstatement, which harmed the Session&#x27;s good name. It also found no due-process irregularity or prejudice warranting reversal, deferring to the lower court under BCO 39-3, leaving indefinite suspension in place.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1998-09" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-10" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1998-10 Curtis v. Eastern Carolina" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1998-10: Curtis v. Eastern Carolina, M28GA, pp. 236–237" data-search-text="1998-10 Curtis v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery Eastern Carolina Presbytery referred to the SJC both TE Byron Curtis&#x27;s complaint against Presbytery&#x27;s order barring him from teaching his exceptions and TE Jeff Black&#x27;s already-sustained complaint on the same subject. Without reaching the merits, the SJC remanded to the Presbytery for adjudication at the next stated meeting, directing that Curtis&#x27;s complaint be heard. It reasoned that judicial complaints in process cannot be referred for mere advice and that, despite uncertainty about what the Presbytery sought, the lower court should hear the case first. Five SJC members dissented; the merits remained open. judicial_reference Remanded Not reached — BCO 43-1, BCO 43-2 reference exceptions to Westminster Confession of Faith exceptions to BCO six-day creation ordination exceptions teaching exceptions prohibition on teaching exceptions presbytery jurisdiction complaint case in process panel">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1998-10</code> <span>· Judicial reference</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga28_2000__1998-10.html">Curtis v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1998-10">Eastern Carolina Presbytery referred to the SJC both TE Byron Curtis&#x27;s complaint against Presbytery&#x27;s order barring him from teaching his exceptions and TE Jeff Black&#x27;s already-sustained complaint on the same subject. Without reaching the merits, the SJC remanded to the Presbytery for adjudication at the next stated meeting, directing that Curtis&#x27;s complaint be heard. It reasoned that judicial complaints in process cannot be referred for mere advice and that, despite uncertainty about what the Presbytery sought, the lower court should hear the case first. Five SJC members dissented; the merits remained open.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1998-10" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Grace Presbytery, was withdrawn by the complainant in the 26th Assembly records. No merits opinion was published, and the available notice does not identify the challenged presbytery action, the grounds, or any reason for withdrawal. The practical effect was that the matter ended without any merits ruling or relief. It illustrates that a bare withdrawal entry supports only a status synopsis, not an inference about the merits.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-02 Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-02: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain, M26GA, pp. 122–128" data-search-text="1997-02 Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement. appeal Remanded Not reached legacy 1997-2 BCO 13-9.a, BCO 38-1, BCO 34-4, BCO 32-6, BCO 35-12, BCO 15-2, BCO 15-3, BCO 42-8, BCO 42-9, BCO 43-1 due process contumacy ecclesiastical discipline deposition from ministry Book of Church Order interpretation trial procedures">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-02</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-02.html">Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-02">Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-03" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-03 Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-03: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain, M26GA, p. 129" data-search-text="1997-03 Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain Bruce Nickoley complained against Rocky Mountain Presbytery over its action dissolving the relationship with Evergreen Church. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order under SJC Manual 10.1. The same matter was already the subject of an appeal granted to Evergreen Church and docketed for Presbytery&#x27;s January 22–24, 1997 meeting, and BCO 43-1 provides that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case in which an appeal is taken. No merits ruling was reached. complaint Administratively out of order; Remanded Not reached legacy 1997-3 BCO 13-9.a, BCO 38-1, BCO 34-4, BCO 32-6, BCO 35-12, BCO 43-1, BCO 42-5 due process rights contumacy charge presbytery powers trial procedure judicial process deposition from ministry">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-03</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-03.html">Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain</a></h3></header>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-04" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-04 Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-04: Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina, M26GA, pp. 129–131" data-search-text="1997-04 Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery&#x27;s denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The SJC upheld Presbytery&#x27;s action. It concluded that the record showed no unconstitutional procedure or BCO violation and that it could consider only facts properly in the record, not material from earlier cases offered in oral argument. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed. appeal Not sustained Not stated legacy 1997-4 BCO 43-1, BCO 31-7, BCO 42-9, BCO 32-4, BCO 35-1, BCO 35-5 church membership rolls presbytery authority complaint procedure due process constitutional procedure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-04</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-04.html">Nancy A. <p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">

<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-04">After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery&#x27;s denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The SJC upheld Presbytery&#x27;s action. It concluded that the record showed no unconstitutional procedure or BCO violation and that it could consider only facts properly in the record, not material from earlier cases offered in oral argument. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-04" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Carmel Session challenged New Jersey Presbytery&#x27;s creation-days resolution, arguing that the Westminster Standards require six consecutive twenty-four-hour days. The SJC majority concluded that Presbytery could resolve the doctrinal question under BCO 11-4 and that prior Assembly actions permitted latitude on the length of the creation days. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-06" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-06 Fitzsimmons v. Evangel" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-06: Fitzsimmons v. Evangel, M26GA, pp. 131–133" data-search-text="1997-06 Fitzsimmons v. Evangel Presbytery After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues. appeal Remanded Not reached legacy 1997-6 BCO 42-9, BCO 42-8, BCO 42-3, BCO 42-5, BCO 15-2, BCO 15-3 appeal procedure due process notice requirements excommunication church discipline procedural error">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-06</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-06.html">Fitzsimmons v. Evangel Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-06">After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. Presbytery found the appeal in order and appointed a commission, but then rescinded that action and never adjudicated the appeal. The SJC held Presbytery erred by failing to notify the appellant of the appeal hearing and by failing to adjudicate an appeal properly before it. It remanded under BCO 42-9 for proper adjudication and made no ruling on the remaining session-related merits issues.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-06" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Central Florida Presbytery The Standing Judicial Commission held Steve Farris&#x27;s complaint against Central Florida Presbytery judicially out of order because Farris was not a member of a PCA church and therefore lacked standing before the Commission. The Commission reached no merits issue and granted no relief; the only stated ground was the complainant&#x27;s lack of standing. The case illustrates a threshold standing bar for SJC complainants, but the sparse record does not identify the underlying presbytery action complained of. complaint Judicially out of order Not reached legacy 1997-7 None listed standing church membership judicial order">

<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Judicially out of order</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-07">The Standing Judicial Commission held Steve Farris&#x27;s complaint against Central Florida Presbytery judicially out of order because Farris was not a member of a PCA church and therefore lacked standing before the Commission. The Commission reached no merits issue and granted no relief; the only stated ground was the complainant&#x27;s lack of standing. The case illustrates a threshold standing bar for SJC complainants, but the sparse record does not identify the underlying presbytery action complained of.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-07" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-09" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-09 Shive v. Central Carolina" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-09: Shive v. Central Carolina, M26GA, pp. 134–143" data-search-text="1997-09 Robert M. Shive v. Central Carolina Presbytery A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance. appeal Reversed; Remanded Great deference unless clear error (factual findings) legacy 1997-9 BCO 30-4, BCO 31-7, BCO 32-17, BCO 32-19, BCO 33-3, BCO 36-5, BCO 42-9 appeal excommunication indefinite suspension ministerial discipline sexual misconduct censure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-09</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-09.html">Robert M. Shive v. Central Carolina Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Reversed; Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-09">A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-09" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-13" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-13 Session of Harvestwood PCA v. New River (Complaint)" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-13: Session of Harvestwood PCA v. New River (Complaint), M26GA, pp. 144–148" data-search-text="1997-13 Session of Harvestwood PCA v. New River Presbytery (Complaint) New River Presbytery treated Grace Covenant PCA&#x27;s BCO 41 inquiry about a Sunday school teacher&#x27;s acceptability as a request for advice, but then ruled he was eligible to teach. On Harvestwood&#x27;s complaint, the SJC held that Presbytery lacked original jurisdiction to make that final disposition and that the record was unclear about the teacher&#x27;s views. The SJC sustained the complaint and recommended that Presbytery rescind its March 15, 1997 action and clarify his views through proper BCO procedures; it declined to reach the creation and theistic-evolution merits. complaint Sustained Not stated — BCO 15-5.a, BCO 15-5.b, BCO 12-5, BCO 41-3, BCO 41-4, BCO 41-6, BCO 39-3, BCO 42-2 Presbytery jurisdiction Reference seeking advice Record of case adequacy Sunday school teacher qualifications Doctrinal standards Theistic evolution Westminster Confession of Faith">

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-16" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1997-16 Session, BPC, Concord, NC v. Central Carolina (Complaint)" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1997-16: Session, BPC, Concord, NC v. Central Carolina (Complaint), M26GA, pp. 148–157" data-search-text="1997-16 Session, BPC, Concord, NC v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Complaint) The Session of Bible Presbyterian Church, Concord, complained that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly accepted its moderator&#x27;s ruling making RE Chris Dollar&#x27;s interim Candidates Committee appointment &quot;null and void&quot; because Christ Covenant Session never approved it. The SJC answered both issues no and did not sustain the complaint, leaving Presbytery&#x27;s action undisturbed. It reasoned that approval was conditional under CCP rules, the moderator expressed Presbytery&#x27;s intention, Presbytery did not surrender jurisdiction, and BCO 39-3 required deference; it found no appearance of prejudice. Vote 11-7, with dissents urging remand and challenging sessional control over committee eligibility. complaint Not sustained Not stated — BCO 39-3 church discipline presbytery action">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1997-16</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga26_1998__1997-16.html">Session, BPC, Concord, NC v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Complaint)</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-16">The Session of Bible Presbyterian Church, Concord, complained that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly accepted its moderator&#x27;s ruling making RE Chris Dollar&#x27;s interim Candidates Committee appointment &quot;null and void&quot; because Christ Covenant Session never approved it. The SJC answered both issues no and did not sustain the complaint, leaving Presbytery&#x27;s action undisturbed. It reasoned that approval was conditional under CCP rules, the moderator expressed Presbytery&#x27;s intention, Presbytery did not surrender jurisdiction, and BCO 39-3 required deference; it found no appearance of prejudice. Vote 11-7, with dissents urging remand and challenging sessional control over committee eligibility.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-16" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1997-17">A member challenged Presbytery’s approval of a congregational motion supplementing an assistant-pastor fund, alleging that Session had ceded its budget authority. The SJC denied both issues. The motion addressed a special circumstance, not approval of the budget, and left the salary figure to the elders and deacons; Session had already approved the budget and retained control of church funds. The ruling was confined to the congregation’s particular circumstances and did not approve congregational budget adoption.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1997-17" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1995-10" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1995-10 Merriam v. Tennessee Valley (Appeal)" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1995-10: Merriam v. Tennessee Valley (Appeal), M25GA, pp. 76–80" data-search-text="1995-10 Stuart Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery (Appeal) After Tennessee Valley Presbytery deposed a minister without conducting a church trial, he appealed, alleging denial of PCA due process. The SJC remanded for a new trial. It held that Presbytery could bring charges but could not substitute the Papua New Guinea criminal proceedings for ecclesiastical process, especially when it neither served an indictment and charges nor appointed counsel for an accused unable to attend. The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline. appeal Remanded Not reached — BCO 31-2, BCO 32-3, BCO 32-6, BCO 34-4, BCO 32-20, BCO 35-3 due process ecclesiastical discipline criminal conviction appeal jurisdiction counsel rights suspension of teaching elder deposition from office procedural violations">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1995-10</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga25_1997__1995-10.html">Stuart Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery (Appeal)</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1995-10">After Tennessee Valley Presbytery deposed a minister without conducting a church trial, he appealed, alleging denial of PCA due process. The SJC remanded for a new trial. It held that Presbytery could bring charges but could not substitute the Papua New Guinea criminal proceedings for ecclesiastical process, especially when it neither served an indictment and charges nor appointed counsel for an accused unable to attend. The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1995-10" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1995-11" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1995-11 Landrum v. Mississippi Valley" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1995-11: Landrum v. Mississippi Valley, M25GA, pp. 80–81" data-search-text="1995-11 James Landrum v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery Complainants challenged Mississippi Valley Presbytery’s approval of James Blaha’s ordination examination, arguing that his views on tongues and prophecy were constitutional exceptions and precluded approval. The SJC agreed that Presbytery should have acknowledged and noted the exceptions, but upheld the examination. It found no proof that Blaha’s denial that the gifts conveyed revelation crossed prior Assembly limits and deferred to Presbytery on an unsettled issue. It expressly declined reexamination or remand; a substantial partial dissent would have set the examination aside. complaint Sustained Not stated — BCO 15-5 ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1995-11</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga25_1997__1995-11.html">James Landrum v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1995-11">Complainants challenged Mississippi Valley Presbytery’s approval of James Blaha’s ordination examination, arguing that his views on tongues and prophecy were constitutional exceptions and precluded approval. The SJC agreed that Presbytery should have acknowledged and noted the exceptions, but upheld the examination. It found no proof that Blaha’s denial that the gifts conveyed revelation crossed prior Assembly limits and deferred to Presbytery on an unsettled issue. It expressly declined reexamination or remand; a substantial partial dissent would have set the examination aside.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1995-11" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1993-01" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1993-01 Smith v. Northeast" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1993-01: Smith v. Northeast, M22GA, pp. 96–106" data-search-text="1993-01 Smith v. Northeast Presbytery Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery&#x27;s objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith&#x27;s protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral &#x27;power of order&#x27; from judicial &#x27;power of jurisdiction,&#x27; the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery&#x27;s efforts satisfied any duty. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1993-1 BCO 3-2, BCO 3-4, BCO 5-2, BCO 5-3, BCO 11-1, BCO 11-4, BCO 25-12, BCO 31-1, BCO 43-3, BCO 45-5 dissolved congregation presbytery administrative commission church membership jurisdiction complaint procedure constitutional rights">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1993-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga22_1994__1993-01.html">Smith v. Northeast Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1993-01">Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery&#x27;s objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith&#x27;s protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral &#x27;power of order&#x27; from judicial &#x27;power of jurisdiction,&#x27; the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery&#x27;s efforts satisfied any duty.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1993-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1993-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1993-02 Johnson v. Evangel" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1993-02: Johnson v. Evangel, M22GA, pp. 107–109" data-search-text="1993-02 Johnson v. Evangel Presbytery An appeal challenged Evangel Presbytery&#x27;s judgment that a teaching elder wrongfully pursued divorce without biblical grounds, alleging procedural irregularities, refused evidence, haste, prejudice, and mistaken censure. The SJC rejected each claim: failure to swear two minor witnesses was acknowledged and nonprejudicial, notices and defense opportunity were adequate, and the guilty finding rested on Scripture, WCF 24:6, BCO 26-1, and 30-3; the 1992 study did not authorize divorce for alleged spiritual desertion. The appeal was not sustained, leaving the indefinite suspension in force; one commissioner dissented. appeal Not sustained Not stated legacy 1993-2 BCO 26-1, BCO 30-3 appeal divorce spiritual desertion church discipline Westminster Confession 24.6">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1993-02</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga22_1994__1993-02.html">Johnson v. Evangel Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1993-02">An appeal challenged Evangel Presbytery&#x27;s judgment that a teaching elder wrongfully pursued divorce without biblical grounds, alleging procedural irregularities, refused evidence, haste, prejudice, and mistaken censure. The SJC rejected each claim: failure to swear two minor witnesses was acknowledged and nonprejudicial, notices and defense opportunity were adequate, and the guilty finding rested on Scripture, WCF 24:6, BCO 26-1, and 30-3; the 1992 study did not authorize divorce for alleged spiritual desertion. The appeal was not sustained, leaving the indefinite suspension in force; one commissioner dissented.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1993-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1993-14" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1993-14 Grace RPC Session v. Heartland" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1993-14: Grace RPC Session v. Heartland, M23GA, pp. 113–117" data-search-text="1993-14 Grace RPC Session v. Heartland Presbytery The Session of Grace Reformed Presbyterian Church appealed its conviction for contumacy and termination of its relationship with Heartland Presbytery. The SJC reversed the conviction, holding that a presbytery lacks original jurisdiction to indict and try a session (lower court) for an offense such as contumacy, as BCO provisions reserve original jurisdiction over ruling elders to the Session level. complaint Affirmed; Reversed; Other Not stated — BCO 13-9, BCO 13-9.b, BCO 15-1, BCO 31-1, BCO 33-1, BCO 40-4, BCO 40-5 presbytery jurisdiction over session contumacy ruling elders original jurisdiction improper indictment of session ecclesiastical power">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1993-14</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga23_1995__1993-12_1993-14.html">Grace RPC Session v. Heartland Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Affirmed; Reversed; Other</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1993-14">The Session of Grace Reformed Presbyterian Church appealed its conviction for contumacy and termination of its relationship with Heartland Presbytery. The SJC reversed the conviction, holding that a presbytery lacks original jurisdiction to indict and try a session (lower court) for an offense such as contumacy, as BCO provisions reserve original jurisdiction over ruling elders to the Session level.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1993-14" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-01" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-01 Smith v. Northeast" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-01: Smith v. Northeast, M21GA, pp. 194–198" data-search-text="1992-01 Smith v. Northeast Presbytery Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility. complaint Sustained; Remanded Not stated legacy 1992-1 BCO 5-1, BCO 11-4, BCO 13-1, BCO 15-5, BCO 25-12, BCO 43-2 standing to complain membership after dissolution pastoral care of dissolved congregation presbytery jurisdiction remand">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga21_1993__1992-01.html">Smith v. Northeast Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained; Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-01">Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-02 Roberts v. New River" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-02: Roberts v. New River, M21GA, pp. 199–209" data-search-text="1992-02 Roberts v. New River Presbytery A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.&#x27;s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation &#x27;shall be accepted&#x27; and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery&#x27;s general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented. complaint Sustained Not stated legacy 1992-2 BCO 13-9, BCO 15-5, BCO 16-2, BCO 21-1, BCO 23-1, BCO 24-6 dissolution of pastoral relationship presbytery authority congregational request ministerial call pastoral care">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-02</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga21_1993__1992-02.html">Roberts v. New River Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-02">A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.&#x27;s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation &#x27;shall be accepted&#x27; and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery&#x27;s general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-03" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-03 Olson, et al. v. Heritage" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-03: Olson, et al. v. Heritage, M20GA, pp. 231–232" data-search-text="1992-03 Richard E. Olson, et al. v. Heritage Presbytery Heritage Presbytery adopted a committee report answering a session&#x27;s reference on whether a session may require officers to abstain from beverage alcohol. Olson and others complained. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order because it was not timely filed with the General Assembly, and independently ruled that a court&#x27;s response to a non-judicial reference seeking advice under BCO 41-3 is not complainable. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-03</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1992-03.html">Richard E. Olson, et al. v. Heritage Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Administratively out of order</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-03">Heritage Presbytery adopted a committee report answering a session&#x27;s reference on whether a session may require officers to abstain from beverage alcohol. Olson and others complained. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order because it was not timely filed with the General Assembly, and independently ruled that a court&#x27;s response to a non-judicial reference seeking advice under BCO 41-3 is not complainable. Complainants may submit their questions to the Committee on Constitutional Business. Confirmed 23-0.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-03" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Administratively out of order; Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-04">Complainants alleged Central Carolina Presbytery failed to act when it remanded their complaints against the Prosperity Presbyterian Church Session to the commission acting as Interim Session. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-05 Parks et al. v. Central Carolina" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-05: Parks et al. v. Central Carolina, M21GA, pp. 210–213" data-search-text="1992-05 Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1992-5 BCO 24-6, BCO 20-6, BCO 20-2, BCO 25-7, BCO 12-5, BCO 23-1, BCO 22-5, BCO 15-3, BCO 24-1, BCO 13-9 ">

<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-06</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga21_1993__1992-06.html">Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery. (Case #1)</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained; Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-06">After a congregation voted to ask that all ruling elders&#x27; official relationships be dissolved without censure, the Session concurred and requested an interim Session. The SJC denied the elders&#x27; complaint, holding that BCO 24-6b extends by good and necessary deduction from one elder to multiple identified elders. Dissolution ended their service on that Session but did not divest them of office. Because both the congregation and Session requested it, BCO 13-9 and 15-2 authorized Presbytery to appoint an interim Session. A separate constitutional inquiry was denied without explanation.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-06" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-07" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-07 Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina (Case #2)" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-07: Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina (Case #2), M21GA, pp. 220–221" data-search-text="1992-07 Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Case #2) A complaint arising from Central Carolina Presbytery’s refusal to prosecute TE Stephen O. Stout and to recognize his accusers as voluntary prosecutors was denied. The SJC framed two issues and answered both yes: the Presbytery could constitutionally adopt its Investigative Committee report and decline judicial process, because the Committee found no “strong presumption of guilt” under BCO 31-2; and it could refuse voluntary-prosecutor status, because BCO 31-1/31-3 left discipline to the Presbytery and made any voluntary prosecutor subject to its approval. The complaint was denied on both issues. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1992-7 BCO 31-2, BCO 45-1, BCO 15-3, BCO 31-6, BCO 31-9, BCO 31-1 ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-07</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga21_1993__1992-07.html">Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Case #2)</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-07">A complaint arising from Central Carolina Presbytery’s refusal to prosecute TE Stephen O. Stout and to recognize his accusers as voluntary prosecutors was denied. The SJC framed two issues and answered both yes: the Presbytery could constitutionally adopt its Investigative Committee report and decline judicial process, because the Committee found no “strong presumption of guilt” under BCO 31-2; and it could refuse voluntary-prosecutor status, because BCO 31-1/31-3 left discipline to the Presbytery and made any voluntary prosecutor subject to its approval. The complaint was denied on both issues.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-07" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-09a" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1992-09a Antioch Session v. Eastern Carolina" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1992-09a: Antioch Session v. Eastern Carolina, M22GA, pp. 88–94" data-search-text="1992-09a Antioch Session v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery Antioch Session challenged Peterson’s licensure based on his prior divorce, creation and local-flood views, reversal of a committee recommendation, and close vote; it also challenged his regular preaching before licensure. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. The licensure remained undisturbed; the ruling was expressly case-specific. complaint Partially sustained Not stated legacy 1992-9a BCO 19-1, BCO 20-5, BCO 22-5, BCO 22-6, BCO 34-5, BCO 43-10 licensure creation age of earth flood (local vs. universal) divorce and remarriage church office qualifications stated supply system of doctrine theonomy presbytery jurisdiction over membership">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-09a</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga22_1994__1992-09a.html">Antioch Session v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-09a">Antioch Session challenged Peterson’s licensure based on his prior divorce, creation and local-flood views, reversal of a committee recommendation, and close vote; it also challenged his regular preaching before licensure. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. The licensure remained undisturbed; the ruling was expressly case-specific.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1992-09a" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1992-10">The Bernards appealed directly to the General Assembly from their excommunication by a Presbytery commission acting as the congregation’s Session. <header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-01.html">Sandra Lovelace v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1991-02" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1991-02 Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1991-02: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest, M20GA, pp. 142–150" data-search-text="1991-02 Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery&#x27;s January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock&#x27;s pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC&#x27;s session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation&#x27;s request. complaint Not sustained Not stated legacy 1991-2 BCO 24-5, BCO 31-1, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-3, BCO 33-1, BCO 11-4, BCO 23-1, BCO 43-4, BCO 43-1, BCO 13-9, BCO 21-1, BCO 24-6, BCO 16-2 presbytery jurisdiction over session session pro tem suspension of session original jurisdiction congregational consent dissolution of pastoral relationship charges against ruling elders commission authority constitutional authority of presbytery">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-02</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-02.html">Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-02">Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery&#x27;s January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock&#x27;s pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC&#x27;s session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation&#x27;s request.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-02" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1991-03" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1991-03 Morse v. Covenant" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1991-03: Morse v. Covenant, M20GA, pp. 154–155" data-search-text="1991-03 Daniel R. Morse v. Covenant Presbytery On Covenant Presbytery’s mixed BCO 41 reference, the SJC held that ministers Morse and Crenshaw could not resign unilaterally; joining another evangelical church invoked BCO 38-3, requiring their names erased, with notice that they were in good standing and faced no pending charges. Grace Church’s withdrawal required a congregational vote, not notice to Presbytery, so its name also was to be erased. Grace had abandoned its complaints, rendering them moot; the SJC nevertheless opined that recording a protest is insulated from complaint by BCO 45-5. judicial_reference Abandoned; Moot Not reached legacy 1991-3 BCO 38-3, BCO 45-5 ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-03</code> <span>· Judicial reference</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-03.html">Daniel R. Morse v. Covenant Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Abandoned; Moot</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-03">On Covenant Presbytery’s mixed BCO 41 reference, the SJC held that ministers Morse and Crenshaw could not resign unilaterally; joining another evangelical church invoked BCO 38-3, requiring their names erased, with notice that they were in good standing and faced no pending charges. Grace Church’s withdrawal required a congregational vote, not notice to Presbytery, so its name also was to be erased. Grace had abandoned its complaints, rendering them moot; the SJC nevertheless opined that recording a protest is insulated from complaint by BCO 45-5.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-03" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1991-04" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1991-04 Hopper v. James River" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1991-04: Hopper v. James River, M20GA, pp. 160–161" data-search-text="1991-04 Robert D. Hopper v. James River Presbytery The SJC denied Hopper&#x27;s complaint against James River Presbytery&#x27;s April 13, 1991 order barring him from teaching or preaching his views on prophecy and tongues. It rejected all five specifications: Scripture did not forbid the order; the 1974 Pastoral Letter did not address presbytery&#x27;s power to enjoin such teaching; forbearance did not preclude protecting peace and purity; presbytery could restrict preaching short of a heresy finding without binding conscience; and allowing presbyteral discussion while restricting congregational teaching was not inconsistent. The action remained in force. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1991-4 None listed ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-04</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-04.html">Robert D. Hopper v. James River Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-04">The SJC denied Hopper&#x27;s complaint against James River Presbytery&#x27;s April 13, 1991 order barring him from teaching or preaching his views on prophecy and tongues. It rejected all five specifications: Scripture did not forbid the order; the 1974 Pastoral Letter did not address presbytery&#x27;s power to enjoin such teaching; forbearance did not preclude protecting peace and purity; presbytery could restrict preaching short of a heresy finding without binding conscience; and allowing presbyteral discussion while restricting congregational teaching was not inconsistent. The action remained in force.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-04" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>
<div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-case__topics-label">Topics</span><span class="judicial-muted">None listed</span></div>
</div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1991-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1991-05 III et al. v. Central Florida" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1991-05: III et al. v. Central Florida, M20GA, pp. 197–202" data-search-text="1991-05 Herman Gunter III et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery Two ruling-elder nominees challenged the Session’s refusal to approve them based on their theonomic views and perceived divisiveness. The full SJC denied the complaint, holding that the court of original jurisdiction may assess an unsettled theological position and whether it threatens the church’s peace, purity, or progress; divisiveness was therefore properly considered. The ruling did not decide the merits of theonomy itself, and it left undisturbed Presbytery’s annulment of the Session’s categorical statement that theonomy violated WCF 19.4. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1991-5 BCO 43-10, BCO 11-3, BCO 11-4 ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-05.html">Herman Gunter III et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-05">Two ruling-elder nominees challenged the Session’s refusal to approve them based on their theonomic views and perceived divisiveness. The full SJC denied the complaint, holding that the court of original jurisdiction may assess an unsettled theological position and whether it threatens the church’s peace, purity, or progress; divisiveness was therefore properly considered. The ruling did not decide the merits of theonomy itself, and it left undisturbed Presbytery’s annulment of the Session’s categorical statement that theonomy violated WCF 19.4.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-05" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-06</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga21_1993__1991-06.html">Lovelace v. <p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Partially sustained</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-06">A member challenged Presbytery’s refusal, after investigation, to try four elders on favoritism charges and its ruling that her related complaint was out of order because dissolution of her church ended her PCA membership. The SJC denied the first item because BCO 31-2 permits declining process when investigation raises no strong presumption of guilt. It sustained the second: jurisdiction properly invoked while a communicant member is not lost through a later status change. No remand was expressly ordered.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-06" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Potomac, M20GA, pp. 214–216" data-search-text="1991-07 Complainants v. Potomac Presbytery Complainants challenged Potomac Presbytery&#x27;s 11/12/91 adjudication denying their complaint over the Timonium Presbyterian Church pastoral dispute, arguing they received too little time, deliberation, and explanation. The SJC held the complaint not sustained: a higher court may not overturn a competent lower court merely because complainants are dissatisfied with the amount of input or time spent, and no constitutional defect was demonstrated. Two earlier complaints were dismissed as not timely filed. The timely 12/11/91 complaint was heard 3/6/92. complaint Not sustained; Dismissed Not stated legacy 1991-7 BCO 43-2 ">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1991-07</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga20_1992__1991-07.html">Complainants v. Potomac Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained; Dismissed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1991-07">Complainants challenged Potomac Presbytery&#x27;s 11/12/91 adjudication denying their complaint over the Timonium Presbyterian Church pastoral dispute, arguing they received too little time, deliberation, and explanation. The SJC held the complaint not sustained: a higher court may not overturn a competent lower court merely because complainants are dissatisfied with the amount of input or time spent, and no constitutional defect was demonstrated. Two earlier complaints were dismissed as not timely filed. The timely 12/11/91 complaint was heard 3/6/92.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1991-07" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

North Texas, M18GA, pp. 363–365" data-search-text="1990-01 First Presbyterian Church of Rowlett, Texas v. North Texas Presbytery A church challenged North Texas Presbytery’s approval of Rev. C. Don Darling, who disclosed that he could not conscientiously accept or conduct remarriage after divorce. The Standing Judicial Commission did not sustain and denied the complaint, affirming Presbytery. Ministerial acceptance ordinarily rests within a presbytery’s jurisdiction, and Darling’s exception neither concerned a fundamental of the doctrinal system nor struck at the vitals of religion or threatened much injury. Overriding Presbytery would therefore improperly impair liberty of conscience. complaint Not sustained; Denied; Affirmed Not stated legacy 1990-1; Case #1 None listed complaint presbytery action minister">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1990-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga18_1990__case1.html">First Presbyterian Church of Rowlett, Texas v. North Texas Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Not sustained; Denied; Affirmed</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1990-01">A church challenged North Texas Presbytery’s approval of Rev. C. Don Darling, who disclosed that he could not conscientiously accept or conduct remarriage after divorce. The Standing Judicial Commission did not sustain and denied the complaint, affirming Presbytery. Ministerial acceptance ordinarily rests within a presbytery’s jurisdiction, and Darling’s exception neither concerned a fundamental of the doctrinal system nor struck at the vitals of religion or threatened much injury. Overriding Presbytery would therefore improperly impair liberty of conscience.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1990-01" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

Eastern Carolina, M19GA, pp. 490–510" data-search-text="1990-04 Chappell v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery&#x27;s Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a &#x27;Session Pro Tem&#x27; without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen. complaint Sustained Not stated legacy 1990-4 BCO 11-2, BCO 11-3, BCO 11-4, BCO 12-5, BCO 13-1, BCO 13-9, BCO 15-1, BCO 15-4, BCO 16-2, BCO 24-1, BCO 24-6, BCO 25-11, BCO 31-1, BCO 33-1, BCO 40-2, BCO 40-4, BCO 40-5, BCO 43-2, BCO 43-9, BCO 46-8, BCO 3-1, BCO 3-2, BCO 3-3, BCO 3-4 presbytery commission powers Session Pro Tem suspension of session without due process limited jurisdiction of church courts ministerial and declarative power congregational right to choose officers ecclesiastical versus civil power Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church delegation of sessional duties complaint ruling elder presbytery action">

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1990-05" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1990-05 Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1990-05: Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley, M19GA, pp. 530–534" data-search-text="1990-05 Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery Complainants challenged the ruling of the session of Westminster Presbyterian Church (Chattanooga) disallowing proxy votes at a December 10, 1989 congregational meeting that voted not to rescind the earlier dissolution and property transfer to New City Fellowship. The SJC denied all specifications, holding that proxy voting was not required under BCO 24-4 or Robert&#x27;s Rules, and that the congregation&#x27;s decision to dissolve was within its rights under BCO Chapter 25. complaint Denied Not stated legacy 1990-5 BCO 24-4, BCO 24-6, BCO 13-9, BCO 11-4, BCO 46-8, BCO 21-5.2, BCO 43-6, BCO 43-2, BCO 46-5, BCO 32-20 proxy voting congregational meeting church dissolution property transfer secret ballot Robert&#x27;s Rules of Order congregational vote higher court authority over local church complaint presbytery action local church">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1990-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga19_1991__1990-05.html">Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1990-05">Complainants challenged the ruling of the session of Westminster Presbyterian Church (Chattanooga) disallowing proxy votes at a December 10, 1989 congregational meeting that voted not to rescind the earlier dissolution and property transfer to New City Fellowship. The SJC denied all specifications, holding that proxy voting was not required under BCO 24-4 or Robert&#x27;s Rules, and that the congregation&#x27;s decision to dissolve was within its rights under BCO Chapter 25.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1990-05" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1990-07" data-judicial-record data-judicial-short-citation="1990-07 Stringer v. Mississippi Valley" data-judicial-full-citation="Case 1990-07: Stringer v. Mississippi Valley, M19GA, pp. 535–538" data-search-text="1990-07 Stringer v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery Randy Stringer appealed his excommunication by Mississippi Valley Presbytery after being deposed and then excommunicated for failure to respond to the presbytery. The SJC set aside the excommunication and remanded the case to MVP, holding that after deposition the presbytery was required under BCO 46-8 to assign Stringer to membership in a particular church rather than proceed to excommunication. Dr. Morton H. Smith dissented, arguing that the presbytery had proper grounds to proceed to excommunication after Stringer&#x27;s contumacy. appeal Sustained; Remanded Not stated legacy 1990-7 BCO 46-8, BCO 13-2, BCO 36-7, BCO 33-1 excommunication deposition membership assignment after deposition church discipline procedure contumacy notification of censure">
<header class="judicial-case__header"><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1990-07</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="/pca-ga/cases/ga19_1991__1990-07.html">Stringer v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery</a></h3></header>
<p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Sustained; Remanded</p>
<div class="judicial-case__layout">
<div class="judicial-case__content">
<div class="judicial-case__summary-wrap"><p class="judicial-case__summary" id="judicial-summary-1990-07">Randy Stringer appealed his excommunication by Mississippi Valley Presbytery after being deposed and then excommunicated for failure to respond to the presbytery. The SJC set aside the excommunication and remanded the case to MVP, holding that after deposition the presbytery was required under BCO 46-8 to assign Stringer to membership in a particular church rather than proceed to excommunication. Dr. Morton H. Smith dissented, arguing that the presbytery had proper grounds to proceed to excommunication after Stringer&#x27;s contumacy.</p><button type="button" class="judicial-case__summary-toggle" aria-controls="judicial-summary-1990-07" aria-expanded="false" hidden>Show full synopsis</button></div>
